Medicine 03.question: ১) Hyper resonant percussion note indicates…...?
Medicine 03.exp:
A hyper-resonant percussion note indicates the presence of excess air in the chest, classically seen in pneumothorax. Air in the pleural space increases resonance on percussion.

Other options:

  • Pneumonia → Causes dull percussion note due to lung consolidation.

  • Hydropneumothorax → Contains both air and fluid; may produce hyper-resonance above and dullness below the fluid level.

  • Pyothorax (empyema) → Causes stony dullness due to pus/fluid accumulation.

Exam pearl:

  • Hyper-resonance → Pneumothorax

  • Stony dullness → Pleural effusion/empyema

  • Dullness → Consolidation (pneumonia).

Medicine 03.question: ২) Honeycomb appearance in X-ray is found in....?
Medicine 03.exp:
A honeycomb appearance on chest X-ray is classically seen in pulmonary fibrosis, especially idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). It represents end-stage interstitial lung disease with destruction of normal lung architecture and formation of multiple small cystic air spaces (honeycomb cysts), usually seen at the lung bases and peripheries.

Other options:

  • Bronchial carcinoma → May show a mass lesion, collapse, or obstructive changes.

  • Bronchiectasis → Shows tram-track shadows, ring shadows, and bronchial dilatation; cystic bronchiectasis may mimic honeycombing but is not classic.

  • Lung abscess → Shows a cavity with an air-fluid level.

Exam pearl:
Honeycomb lung → Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (end-stage interstitial lung disease).

Medicine 03.question: ৩) Which of the following is not true about lung abscess?
Medicine 03.exp:
Lung abscess is usually a unilateral disease, so the statement “usually bilateral” is false.

A lung abscess is a localized collection of pus within the lung parenchyma, usually caused by bacterial infection, commonly following aspiration.

Typical features:

  • Acute process → Common presentation (especially primary lung abscess)

  • High fever → Common due to infection

  • Foul-smelling sputum → Due to anaerobic bacterial infection and tissue necrosis

Other options:

  • Acute process → True

  • High fever → True

  • Foul smelling sputum → True

Exam pearl:
Lung abscess → Usually unilateral + fever + foul-smelling sputum + cavity with air-fluid level on CXR.

Medicine 03.question: ৪) Which is the absolute indication of steroids along with anti-TB drugs?
Medicine 03.exp:
The absolute indication for adding corticosteroids with anti-TB therapy is tuberculous meningitis. Steroids (usually dexamethasone or prednisolone) reduce inflammation and cerebral oedema, thereby decreasing complications such as:

  • Raised intracranial pressure

  • Cranial nerve palsies

  • Neurological disability

  • Mortality

Other options:

  • Tubercular peritonitis → Steroids are not routinely indicated.

  • Tuberculous pericarditis → Steroids may be considered in selected cases but benefit is less clear; not an absolute indication.

  • Bilateral adrenal TB → Requires anti-TB therapy and steroid replacement if adrenal insufficiency is present, but not as adjunct anti-inflammatory therapy.

Exam pearl:
TB meningitis → Anti-TB drugs + corticosteroids (mandatory).

Medicine 03.question: ৫) Which type of bronchial carcinoma is most dangerous?
Medicine 03.exp:
Small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is considered the most dangerous type of bronchial carcinoma because it is:

  • Highly aggressive

  • Has rapid growth

  • Early metastasis (especially to brain, liver, and bone)

  • Usually diagnosed at an advanced stage

  • Strongly associated with smoking

Other options:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma → Common in smokers, usually central, may cause hypercalcaemia (PTHrP).

  • Adenocarcinoma → Most common lung cancer overall but less aggressive than SCLC.

  • Large cell carcinoma → Aggressive but less common.

Exam pearl:
Small-cell carcinoma = most aggressive/dangerous lung cancer + early metastasis + SIADH/ectopic ACTH.

Medicine 03.question: ৬) Which anti-TB drug causes retrobulbar neuritis?
Medicine 03.exp:
Ethambutol is the anti-TB drug that causes retrobulbar neuritis (optic neuritis) due to optic nerve toxicity. It can produce:

  • Reduced visual acuity

  • Red–green colour blindness

  • Central scotoma

Other options:

  • INH (Isoniazid) → Causes peripheral neuropathy due to pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) deficiency.

  • Pyrazinamide → Causes hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia (gout).

  • Streptomycin → Causes 8th cranial nerve toxicity (vestibular/cochlear damage).

Exam pearl:
Ethambutol → Eye toxicity (retrobulbar neuritis + red-green colour blindness)
INH → Peripheral neuropathy
Streptomycin → Ototoxicity.

Medicine 03.question: ৭) Immediate percutaneous needle aspiration is done in....... Intercostal space anteriorly in mid clavicular line?
Medicine 03.exp:
Immediate percutaneous needle aspiration (needle decompression) for tension pneumothorax is traditionally performed in the:

➡️ 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line

The needle is inserted just above the upper border of the 3rd rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

Other options:

  • 3rd, 4th, 5th intercostal spaces → Not the classic emergency needle decompression site (though newer guidelines may use the 4th–5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line for better success).

Exam pearl:
Tension pneumothorax emergency decompression → 2nd ICS, mid-clavicular line (traditional MBBS exam answer).

Medicine 03.question: ৮) Which of the following is not true about pulmonary TB?
Medicine 03.option1: night sweats & evening rise of temperature present
Medicine 03.exp:
Clubbing is not usually present in pulmonary tuberculosis, so this statement is false. Clubbing may occur in some chronic suppurative lung diseases or malignancy, but it is not a typical feature of pulmonary TB.

Other options:

  • Night sweats & evening rise of temperature → True; classic constitutional symptoms of TB.

  • Smoking history not important → True; TB can occur irrespective of smoking history (though smoking increases risk of respiratory infections).

  • Occurs at any age → True; pulmonary TB can affect all age groups.

Exam pearl:
Pulmonary TB features → Evening fever + night sweats + weight loss + chronic cough.
Clubbing is not a usual feature of uncomplicated pulmonary TB.

Medicine 03.question: ৯) Which of the following case is to be treated under category-1 anti-TB treatment regimen?
Medicine 03.exp:
Category-1 anti-TB treatment regimen is used for new TB cases, including:

  • New smear-positive pulmonary TB

  • New smear-negative pulmonary TB with extensive disease

  • Severe extra-pulmonary TB (e.g., TB meningitis, disseminated TB)

Other options:

  • Relapse → Treated under Category-2 regimen (previously treated cases).

  • Treatment failure → Category-2 regimen.

  • Treatment after default → Category-2 regimen.

Exam pearl:
Category-1 = New TB cases
Category-2 = Previously treated TB (Relapse, Failure, Default).

Medicine 03.question: ১০) Which of the following is not a CXR finding in emphysema?
Medicine 03.exp:
In emphysema, there is air trapping and hyperinflation of the lungs, producing characteristic chest X-ray findings:

  • Hypertranslucent lung fields → True (increased air content with reduced vascular markings).

  • Low, flat diaphragm → True (due to lung hyperinflation).

  • Long tubular heart shadow → True (vertical, narrow “teardrop/tubular” heart due to hyperinflated lungs).

Narrowing of rib spaces is not a feature; emphysema causes widening of intercostal spaces due to hyperinflation.

Exam pearl:
Emphysema CXR → Hyperinflation + hyperlucency + flattened diaphragm + widened intercostal spaces + long narrow heart.

Medicine 03.question: ১১) Which organism is most common for atypical pneumonia?
Medicine 03.exp:
The most common cause of atypical pneumonia is Mycoplasma pneumoniae. It is especially common in:

  • Young adults

  • Community outbreaks (e.g., schools, military settings)

Typical features of atypical pneumonia:

  • Dry cough

  • Low-grade fever

  • Minimal chest signs compared with X-ray findings

  • Diffuse interstitial infiltrates

Other options:

  • Chlamydia → Can cause atypical pneumonia but less common.

  • Coxiella burnetii → Causes Q fever pneumonia, uncommon.

  • Influenza → Causes viral pneumonia, not classically the most common “atypical pneumonia” organism.

Exam pearl:
Most common atypical pneumonia organism → Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

Medicine 03.question: ১২) What is the usual duration of rescue therapy for asthma?
Medicine 03.exp:
The usual duration of rescue therapy for asthma exacerbation (typically a short course of oral corticosteroids, e.g., prednisolone) is around 5–7 days in adults. A 7-day course is a commonly used regimen to control acute airway inflammation and prevent relapse.

Other options:

  • 10 days → May be used in some situations but is not the usual duration.

  • 15 days / 30 days → Too long for routine rescue therapy and increases risk of steroid adverse effects.

Exam pearl:
Acute asthma exacerbation → Oral steroid rescue therapy usually for 5–7 days (commonly 7 days).

Medicine 03.question: ১৩) Which investigation is more sensitive to diagnose bronchiectasis?
Medicine 03.exp:
High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest is the most sensitive and investigation of choice for diagnosing bronchiectasis. It directly demonstrates bronchial dilatation and structural changes such as:

  • Increased bronchoarterial ratio (signet ring sign)

  • Lack of bronchial tapering

  • Visible bronchi near pleura

Other options:

  • CXR → May show tram-track and ring shadows but has low sensitivity.

  • Sputum examination → Helps identify infecting organisms, not diagnose bronchiectasis.

  • Serum immunoglobulin → Used to investigate underlying causes (e.g., immunodeficiency).

Exam pearl:
Bronchiectasis diagnosis → HRCT chest = gold standard / investigation of choice.

Medicine 03.question: ১৪) What is the commonest organism for bronchiolitis?
Medicine 03.exp:
The commonest organism causing bronchiolitis (especially in infants and young children) is Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV).

RSV causes:

  • Acute inflammation and obstruction of small airways (bronchioles)

  • Wheezing

  • Cough

  • Tachypnoea and respiratory distress

Other options:

  • Adenovirus → Can cause respiratory infections but is not the commonest cause of bronchiolitis.

  • Rhinovirus → Common cold virus; can trigger wheezing but less common cause of bronchiolitis.

  • Enterovirus → Less commonly involved.

Exam pearl:
Infant bronchiolitis → RSV is the most common pathogen.

Medicine 03.question: ১৫) Which of the following is a cause of type-2 respiratory failure?
Medicine 03.exp:
Type-2 respiratory failure is characterized by raised PaCO₂ (hypercapnia) due to alveolar hypoventilation. Causes are mainly conditions that reduce effective ventilation (“pump failure” or airway obstruction), such as:

  • Upper airway obstruction → Causes inadequate ventilation and CO₂ retention.

  • COPD, neuromuscular disorders, obesity hypoventilation, chest wall disorders are other examples.

Other options:

  • Asthma → Usually causes Type-1 respiratory failure initially; severe/fatal asthma can progress to Type-2.

  • Pneumonia → Classically causes Type-1 respiratory failure due to V/Q mismatch.

  • Aspiration → Usually causes hypoxaemia (Type-1) from aspiration pneumonia.

Exam pearl:
Type-1 respiratory failure → Hypoxia (↓PaO₂) without CO₂ retention (e.g., pneumonia).
Type-2 respiratory failure → Hypoxia + hypercapnia (↑PaCO₂) due to hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, airway obstruction).

Medicine 03.question: ১৬) What is the percentage of oxygen administered in Type-1 respiratory failure?
Medicine 03.exp:
In Type-1 respiratory failure (hypoxaemic respiratory failure), patients have low PaO₂ with normal or low PaCO₂. The main treatment is oxygen therapy, usually given at a higher concentration (around 40–60% oxygen) to correct hypoxaemia.

Examples of Type-1 respiratory failure:

  • Pneumonia

  • Pulmonary oedema

  • Pulmonary embolism

  • ARDS

Other options:

  • 20–40% → May be insufficient in significant hypoxaemia.

  • 24–28% → Used for controlled oxygen therapy in Type-2 respiratory failure (especially COPD with CO₂ retention).

  • 32–36% → Lower concentration; not the typical answer for Type-1 respiratory failure.

Exam pearl:

  • Type-1 respiratory failure → High-flow oxygen (often 40–60%)

  • Type-2 respiratory failure (COPD) → Controlled oxygen 24–28% (Venturi mask).

Medicine 03.question: ১৭) What is the normal amount of pleural fluid?
Medicine 03.exp:
The normal amount of pleural fluid present in the pleural space is less than 25 mL. This small amount of fluid acts as a lubricant, allowing smooth movement of the visceral and parietal pleura during respiration.

Other options:

  • <15 mL → Too low; may be considered within normal range in some references but not the standard exam value.

  • <50 mL / <100 mL → Excessive amounts suggest pleural effusion.

Exam pearl:
Normal pleural fluid volume → <25 mL
Pleural effusion → abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space.

Medicine 03.question: ১৮) Hospital acquired pneumonia is called.........?
Medicine 03.exp:
Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is also called nosocomial pneumonia. It develops 48 hours or more after hospital admission and was not present or incubating at the time of admission.

Other options:

  • Aspiration pneumonia → Caused by inhalation of gastric contents or oropharyngeal secretions.

  • CAP (Community-acquired pneumonia) → Acquired outside the hospital or before admission.

  • Suppurative pneumonia → Refers to pneumonia with pus formation, not hospital origin.

Exam pearl:
Hospital-acquired pneumonia = Nosocomial pneumonia (≥48 hours after admission).

Medicine 03.question: ১৯) Which is the cause of unilateral pleural effusion?
Medicine 03.exp:
Pancreatitis is a cause of unilateral pleural effusion, usually due to inflammation of the pancreas causing:

  • Diaphragmatic irritation

  • Lymphatic obstruction

  • Leakage of pancreatic fluid (pancreaticopleural fistula)

Other options:

  • CCF (Congestive cardiac failure) → Usually causes bilateral pleural effusion (transudative).

  • Nephrotic syndrome (NS) → Usually causes bilateral effusions due to low oncotic pressure.

  • Chronic liver disease (CLD) → Usually causes bilateral effusion (hepatic hydrothorax, commonly right-sided).

Exam pearl:
Unilateral pleural effusion causes → TB, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis.
Bilateral pleural effusion → CCF, nephrotic syndrome, CLD.

Medicine 03.question: ২০) Which of the following is not a feature of bacterial pneumonia?
Medicine 03.exp:
Dry cough is not a typical feature of bacterial pneumonia. Bacterial pneumonia usually presents with a productive cough due to purulent sputum production.

Typical features of bacterial pneumonia:

  • Abrupt onset → True; symptoms often develop suddenly.

  • Features of consolidation → True; bronchial breathing, dullness, increased vocal resonance may occur.

  • Leukocytosis → True; neutrophilic leukocytosis is common due to bacterial infection.

Other options:

  • Dry cough → More commonly seen in atypical pneumonia (e.g., Mycoplasma pneumoniae, viral infections).

Exam pearl:
Typical bacterial pneumonia → Sudden onset + productive cough + consolidation signs + neutrophilic leukocytosis.

Medicine 03.question: ২১) Which is the cause of transudative pleural effusion?
Medicine 03.exp:
A transudative pleural effusion occurs due to systemic factors causing changes in hydrostatic pressure or oncotic pressure, without primary pleural inflammation.

Hypothyroidism can cause transudative pleural effusion due to increased capillary permeability and reduced lymphatic drainage (often with low protein content).

Other options:

  • Pulmonary TB → Causes exudative pleural effusion due to pleural inflammation.

  • Bronchial carcinoma → Causes exudative malignant pleural effusion.

  • Pulmonary infarction (pulmonary embolism) → Usually causes exudative pleural effusion.

Exam pearl:
Transudative effusion causes (think “systemic”):

  • CCF (most common)

  • Cirrhosis

  • Nephrotic syndrome

  • Hypoalbuminaemia
    Exudative effusion: TB, malignancy, pneumonia, PE.

Medicine 03.question: ২২) What is the specific investigation for legionella pneumonia?
Medicine 03.exp:
The specific investigation for Legionella pneumonia is urinary antigen detection. It detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1, which is responsible for most cases of Legionnaires’ disease.

Other options:

  • CXR → Shows pneumonia infiltrates but is not specific.

  • CT chest → More sensitive for lung changes but not diagnostic for Legionella.

  • Sputum study → May be used for culture/PCR but is less commonly used and less rapid.

Exam pearl:
Legionella pneumonia → Urinary antigen test is the specific and rapid diagnostic test.
Associated clues: Hyponatraemia, GI symptoms (diarrhoea), high fever, and relative bradycardia.

Medicine 03.question: ২৩) What will be the percussion note in case of pleural effusion?
Medicine 03.exp:
In pleural effusion, the percussion note is classically stony dull due to the presence of fluid in the pleural cavity, which markedly reduces resonance.

Other options:

  • Resonant → Normal lung percussion note.

  • Dull → Seen in lung consolidation (e.g., pneumonia).

  • Woody dull → Classically described in some cases of massive pleural effusion or thick pleural fluid, but the standard exam answer for pleural effusion is stony dull.

Exam pearl:

  • Pleural effusion → Stony dull percussion note

  • Pneumothorax → Hyper-resonant note

  • Lung consolidation → Dull note.

Medicine 03.question: ২৪) Predominant lymphocytes in pleural fluid study indicates......?
Medicine 03.exp:
A lymphocyte-predominant pleural fluid is classically associated with tuberculous pleural effusion. TB causes a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response, leading to predominance of lymphocytes in pleural fluid.

Other options:

  • Pneumonia → Usually causes neutrophil-predominant exudative pleural effusion (parapneumonic effusion).

  • Bronchial carcinoma → Can cause lymphocyte-rich effusion, especially malignant effusions, but TB is the classic exam answer.

  • Lung abscess → Usually associated with neutrophilic inflammation.

Exam pearl:
Pleural fluid cell type:

  • Lymphocyte predominant → TB (classic), malignancy

  • Neutrophil predominant → Acute infection (pneumonia, empyema).

Medicine 03.question: ২৫) What is the maximum amount of pleural fluid that can be drawn at a time?
Medicine 03.exp:
The maximum amount of pleural fluid that should be removed at one time during therapeutic thoracentesis is about 1.5 litres. Removing larger volumes increases the risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema (REPO) due to sudden re-expansion of a chronically compressed lung.

Other options:

  • 0.5 L → Too low; not the usual maximum limit.

  • 1.0 L → Often a cautious volume, but not the standard maximum exam answer.

  • 2.0 L → Too high; increases risk of re-expansion injury.

Exam pearl:
Thoracentesis → Do not remove >1.5 L pleural fluid at a time (to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema).

Medicine 03.question: ২৬) Which pneumothorax is worst of all?
Medicine 03.exp:
Tension pneumothorax is the worst and most life-threatening type of pneumothorax because air enters the pleural space but cannot escape (one-way valve mechanism). This causes progressive increase in intrathoracic pressure leading to:

  • Compression of the affected lung

  • Mediastinal shift

  • Reduced venous return to the heart

  • Obstructive shock

  • Cardiovascular collapse

Other options:

  • Closed pneumothorax → Air enters pleural space without an open chest wound; may be mild.

  • Open pneumothorax → Communication with atmosphere (“sucking chest wound”), but less dangerous than tension pneumothorax.

  • Traumatic pneumothorax → Can be serious, but severity depends on the injury.

Exam pearl:
Most dangerous pneumothorax → Tension pneumothorax
Emergency treatment → Immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion.

Medicine 03.question: ২৭) Which bronchial carcinoma is radiosensitive??
Medicine 03.exp:
Small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is the most radiosensitive type of bronchial carcinoma. It is a high-grade neuroendocrine tumour with rapid growth and early metastasis, but it responds well to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Other options:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma → Less radiosensitive; often treated with surgery if localized.

  • Adenocarcinoma → Not the most radiosensitive; commonest type of lung cancer.

  • Large cell carcinoma → Aggressive tumour with poor prognosis, not particularly radiosensitive.

Exam pearl:
Most radiosensitive lung cancer → Small cell carcinoma (SCLC).
Most common lung cancer → Adenocarcinoma.

Medicine 03.question: ২৮) Which isn't a usual sign of bronchial asthma?
Medicine 03.option4: evidence of allergic nasal, sinus or skin diseases
Medicine 03.exp:
Inspiratory rhonchi is not a usual sign of bronchial asthma. Asthma is primarily an expiratory airway obstruction disease, so the characteristic auscultatory finding is:

  • Expiratory wheeze (rhonchi) due to narrowing of small airways during expiration.

Other options:

  • Tachypnoea → True; may occur during acute asthma attacks.

  • Cyanosis → True in severe or life-threatening asthma due to hypoxaemia.

  • Evidence of allergic nasal, sinus, or skin diseases → True; asthma is commonly associated with atopy (allergic rhinitis, eczema).

Exam pearl:
Asthma → Expiratory wheeze + prolonged expiration + atopic features.
Inspiratory sounds suggest upper airway obstruction or other pathology, not typical asthma.

Medicine 03.question: ২৯) Goals of management of bronchial asthma excludes...?
Medicine 03.option3: prevent development of reversible airflow limitation
Medicine 03.option4: avoid adverse effects from asthma medications
Medicine 03.exp:
The goals of bronchial asthma management (as per GINA principles) are to:

  • Achieve and maintain control of symptoms 

  • Prevent exacerbations and reduce future risk 

  • Maintain normal activity levels and lung function 

  • Avoid adverse effects from asthma medications 

Prevent development of reversible airflow limitation is not a management goal, because asthma is already characterized by variable, usually reversible airflow limitation. Treatment aims to control and prevent worsening/remodelling, not prevent the initial development of reversible obstruction.

Exam pearl:
Asthma management goals → Symptom control + prevent exacerbations + maintain lung function + minimize drug side effects.

Medicine 03.question: ৩০) Which isn't a criteria of status asthmaticus?
Medicine 03.option4: Inability to complete sentences in 1 breath
Medicine 03.exp:
Status asthmaticus refers to a severe, prolonged asthma exacerbation that does not respond adequately to usual bronchodilator therapy. Criteria suggesting acute severe asthma include:

  • PEF 33–50% predicted → indicates acute severe asthma, not status asthmaticus specifically.

  • Respiratory rate ≥25/min → True criterion of acute severe asthma.

  • Heart rate ≥100/min → True criterion of acute severe asthma.

  • Inability to complete sentences in one breath → True; suggests severe airflow obstruction.

For status asthmaticus / life-threatening asthma, features include:

  • Silent chest

  • Cyanosis

  • Exhaustion

  • Altered consciousness

  • Rising PaCO₂

Exam pearl:
Acute severe asthma: PEF 33–50%, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, unable to complete sentences.
Life-threatening asthma: Silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, raised PaCO₂.

Medicine 03.question: ৩১) Daily steroid tablet is recommended for which step of management of asthma control?
Medicine 03.exp:
Daily oral steroid (maintenance oral corticosteroid) is recommended only in Step 5 asthma management for patients with severe asthma that remains uncontrolled despite maximal inhaled therapy.

Step-wise asthma management (simplified):

  • Step 1: As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol

  • Step 2: Low-dose ICS maintenance

  • Step 3: Low-dose ICS + LABA

  • Step 4: Medium-dose ICS + LABA

  • Step 5: Add-on therapies (biologics, specialist referral, and maintenance oral corticosteroids if needed)

Other options:

  • Step 2, 3, 4 → Managed mainly with inhaled corticosteroids ± LABA; routine daily oral steroids are not recommended due to adverse effects.

Exam pearl:
Chronic daily oral steroid in asthma → Step 5 (severe refractory asthma).

Medicine 03.question: ৩২) Which isn't a predisposing factor of pneumonia?
Medicine 03.exp:
Child age group is not considered a predisposing factor for pneumonia in general. Although children (especially infants) can develop pneumonia due to immature immunity, “child age group” alone is not a classic risk factor listed for pneumonia in adults.

Predisposing factors for pneumonia include:

  • Cigarette smoking → Impairs mucociliary clearance and increases infection risk.

  • Upper respiratory tract infections (URTI) → Damage airway defenses and predispose to lower respiratory infection.

  • Alcohol → Increases aspiration risk and impairs immune function.

Exam pearl:
Pneumonia risk factors → Smoking + alcohol + impaired immunity + aspiration + chronic lung disease.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৩) Following are the features of pneumonia excludes...?
Medicine 03.exp:
Vesicular breath sound is not a typical feature of pneumonia. In pneumonia, especially with lung consolidation, normal vesicular breathing is replaced by bronchial breathing due to increased transmission of sound through solidified lung tissue.

Features of pneumonia:

  • Tachycardia → True; occurs due to fever, hypoxia, and systemic response.

  • Tachypnoea → True; common due to respiratory distress.

  • Toxic look → True; especially in severe bacterial pneumonia due to systemic infection.

Exam pearl:
Pneumonia with consolidation → Bronchial breath sound + dull percussion note + increased vocal resonance.
Normal lung → Vesicular breath sound.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৪) What your clinical finding in a patient with right sided pleural effusion?
Medicine 03.option1: restricted chest movement in left side
Medicine 03.option2: vocal fremitus reduced in left side
Medicine 03.option4: breath sound diminished in left side
Medicine 03.exp:
In right-sided pleural effusion, accumulation of fluid in the right pleural cavity causes compression of the right lung. If the effusion is large (massive pleural effusion), the increased volume pushes the mediastinal structures, causing the trachea to shift to the opposite side (left side).

Clinical findings of right-sided pleural effusion:

  • Reduced chest expansion on the right side  (not left)

  • Reduced vocal fremitus on the right side  (fluid blocks sound transmission)

  • Dull/stony dull percussion note on the right side

Other options:

  • Restricted chest movement in left side → Incorrect; should be right side.

  • Vocal fremitus reduced in left side → Incorrect; should be right side.

  • Breath sound diminished in left side → Incorrect; should be right side.

Exam pearl:
Massive pleural effusion → Trachea shifts away from the affected side.
Right pleural effusion → Trachea shifts left.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৫) Deficiency of which vitamin is a risk factor for Tuberculosis?
Medicine 03.exp:
Vitamin A deficiency is associated with an increased risk of tuberculosis (TB) because vitamin A plays an important role in:

  • Maintaining mucosal immunity

  • Supporting T-cell–mediated immune response

  • Enhancing macrophage function against Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Deficiency can impair host defense and increase susceptibility to TB infection.

Other options:

  • Vitamin B → Not a major recognized risk factor for TB.

  • Vitamin C → Has immune-supporting roles but deficiency is not a classic TB risk factor.

  • Vitamin K → Mainly involved in coagulation; not related to TB susceptibility.

Exam pearl:
Risk factors for TB → HIV, malnutrition, diabetes mellitus, smoking, alcoholism, and vitamin A deficiency.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৬) Causes of secondary pneumothorax excludes...?
Medicine 03.exp:
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs due to an underlying lung disease. Common causes include:

  • COPD  (most common cause; especially emphysema)

  • Tuberculosis  (can cause cavitary lung destruction leading to pneumothorax)

  • Rupture of emphysematous bulla  (classic mechanism in emphysema)

Lung abscess is not a usual cause of secondary pneumothorax. Although rare complications such as bronchopleural fistula can occur, it is not considered a typical cause.

Exam pearl:
Secondary pneumothorax causes → COPD, TB, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, lung malignancy.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৭) Which LFT isn't measured by spirometer?
Medicine 03.exp:
Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) is not measured by a spirometer; it is measured using a peak flow meter.

Other options:

  • VC (Vital Capacity)  → Measured by spirometry.

  • FEV₁ (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second)  → Measured by spirometry; important for diagnosing obstructive lung disease.

  • FVC (Forced Vital Capacity)  → Measured by spirometry.

Exam pearl:
Spirometry measures → FEV₁, FVC, VC, FEV₁/FVC ratio.
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) → Peak flow meter.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৮) Which anti TB drug causes hyperuricemia?
Medicine 03.exp:
Pyrazinamide is the anti-TB drug most commonly associated with hyperuricaemia. It reduces renal excretion of uric acid, leading to increased serum uric acid levels and may precipitate gout.

Other options:

  • INH (Isoniazid) → Causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis; not hyperuricaemia.

  • Rifampicin → Causes hepatotoxicity, orange discoloration of body fluids, and drug interactions.

  • Ethambutol → Causes optic neuritis (retrobulbar neuritis) with visual impairment.

Exam pearl:
Anti-TB adverse effects:

  • Pyrazinamide → Hyperuricaemia + hepatotoxicity

  • Ethambutol → Optic neuritis (red-green colour blindness)

  • INH → Peripheral neuropathy + hepatitis

  • Rifampicin → Orange body fluids + hepatotoxicity.

Medicine 03.question: ৩৯) Which one isn't correct about 4FDC of anti TB drug?
Medicine 03.exp:
A standard 4-drug fixed-dose combination (4FDC) of anti-TB therapy contains:

  • Isoniazid (INH) → 75 mg ✅

  • Rifampicin → 150 mg ✅

  • Pyrazinamide → 400 mg 

  • Ethambutol → 275 mg (approximately, in standard adult FDC)  if stated as 300 mg in this context

However, among the given options, the incorrect standard dose is Pyrazinamide 400 mg, because in the commonly used adult 4FDC tablet, Pyrazinamide is usually 400 mg per tablet but the dose varies according to weight, so some exam keys consider this option incorrect when referring to the standard formulation.

Medicine 03.question: ৪০) A patient present with chronic cough, productive copious purulent sputum, digital clubbing, coarse crepitation. What is the best possible diagnosis?
Medicine 03.exp:
The combination of chronic productive cough with copious purulent sputum, digital clubbing, and coarse crepitations is highly suggestive of bronchiectasis.

Bronchiectasis is characterized by permanent dilatation of bronchi due to chronic airway inflammation and infection, leading to:

  • Large amounts of foul/purulent sputum production

  • Recurrent chest infections

  • Coarse crackles (crepitations)

  • Digital clubbing (in severe disease)

Other options:

  • Lung abscess → Usually presents with acute fever, toxicity, and foul-smelling sputum; not typically chronic with clubbing.

  • Bronchial carcinoma → May cause cough and clubbing but copious purulent sputum with coarse crepitations is less typical.

  • Pulmonary TB → Chronic cough and clubbing may occur, but massive purulent sputum production is more characteristic of bronchiectasis.

Exam pearl:
Bronchiectasis triad → Chronic cough + copious purulent sputum + coarse crackles (± clubbing).

Medicine 03.question: ৪১) Non metastatic neurological manifestation due to bronchial carcinoma excludes?
Medicine 03.exp:
The question asks for a non-metastatic neurological manifestation due to bronchial carcinoma that is excluded.

In bronchial carcinoma (especially small-cell lung carcinoma), common non-metastatic neurological paraneoplastic syndromes include:

  • Polyneuropathy ✅

  • Subacute cerebellar degeneration (cerebral/cerebellar degeneration) ✅

  • Myelopathy (rare paraneoplastic spinal cord involvement) ✅

Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is also a classic paraneoplastic neurological syndrome of small-cell lung cancer, but it is usually considered a neuromuscular junction disorder, not simply a neurological manifestation in some exam classifications.

Exam pearl:
Small-cell lung carcinoma paraneoplastic syndromes → LEMS (most classic), SIADH, Cushing syndrome, cerebellar degeneration.

Medicine 03.question: ৪২) Which drug is used for Anti IgE therapy?
Medicine 03.exp:
Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used as a targeted therapy in severe allergic asthma. It binds to circulating IgE, preventing IgE from attaching to mast cells and basophils, thereby reducing allergic airway inflammation.

Other options:

  • Triamcinolone → Inhaled/systemic corticosteroid; reduces inflammation but does not target IgE.

  • Zileuton → 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor; decreases leukotriene synthesis.

  • Flunisolide → Inhaled corticosteroid used for asthma control.

Exam pearl:
Anti-IgE therapy in asthma → Omalizumab.
Anti-IL-5 therapies → Mepolizumab, Reslizumab, Benralizumab.

Medicine 03.question: ৪৩) COPD is usually featured by...?
Medicine 03.exp:
COPD (especially emphysema) is characterized by hyperinflation and air trapping, leading to:

  • Reduced chest expansion ✅ due to hyperinflated lungs and decreased diaphragmatic movement.

  • Increased anteroposterior chest diameter (barrel chest)

  • Hyper-resonant percussion note

  • Reduced breath sounds

Other options:

  • Dull percussion note  → Seen in consolidation or pleural effusion, not COPD.

  • Clubbing  → Not a feature of COPD; suggests malignancy, bronchiectasis, or interstitial lung disease.

  • Bronchial breath sound  → Seen in lung consolidation (e.g., pneumonia).

Exam pearl:
COPD examination findings → Hyper-resonant percussion + reduced breath sounds + prolonged expiration + reduced chest expansion.

Medicine 03.question: ৪৪) Which one isn't a component of CURB-65 score to assess severity of pneumonia?
Medicine 03.exp:
The CURB-65 score is used to assess the severity and mortality risk of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

CURB-65 components:

  • C – Confusion 

  • U – Urea > 7 mmol/L  (not >5 mmol/L)

  • R – Respiratory rate ≥30/min 

  • B – Blood pressure low (SBP <90 mmHg or DBP ≤60 mmHg)

  • 65 – Age ≥65 years 

Therefore, Urea >5 mmol/L is not a correct component of CURB-65.

Exam pearl:
CURB-65 = Confusion + Urea (>7 mmol/L) + RR ≥30 + low Blood pressure + Age ≥65.

Medicine 03.question: ৪৫) In alveolar cell carcinoma, which type of sputum is usually found?
Medicine 03.exp:
Alveolar cell carcinoma (bronchioloalveolar carcinoma; a subtype of adenocarcinoma) characteristically produces serous, watery sputum because the tumour arises from type II pneumocytes/bronchiolar epithelial cells and may produce large amounts of watery mucus-like fluid.

Other options:

  • Mucoid → More commonly seen in adenocarcinoma with mucin production.

  • Purulent → Suggests infection such as bronchiectasis, lung abscess, or bacterial pneumonia.

  • Rusty sputum → Classically seen in pneumococcal pneumonia due to blood degradation products.

Exam pearl:
Bronchioloalveolar (alveolar cell) carcinoma → copious watery/serous sputum production.

Medicine 03.question: ৪৬) 'Breathlessness increases due to walking in the morning' in which of the following condition?
Medicine 03.exp:
In COPD, breathlessness typically increases with exertion, such as walking, because airflow limitation and air trapping reduce the ability to increase ventilation during physical activity. Patients often complain of progressive exertional dyspnoea, especially during activities like walking or climbing stairs.

Other options:

  • Pulmonary fibrosis → Also causes exertional breathlessness, but the classic association is dry cough, fine end-inspiratory crepitations, and restrictive lung pattern.

  • Pulmonary TB → Usually presents with chronic cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss; exertional dyspnoea is not the typical feature.

  • Pleural effusion → Causes breathlessness due to fluid accumulation, but the symptom is not classically described as increasing specifically with morning walking.

Exam pearl:
COPD → Progressive exertional breathlessness + chronic cough + sputum production + wheeze.

Medicine 03.question: ৪৭) All of the following are spontaneous pneumothorax except...?
Medicine 03.exp:
Iatrogenic pneumothorax is not a spontaneous pneumothorax because it occurs due to a medical procedure or intervention, such as:

  • Central venous catheter insertion

  • Transthoracic needle biopsy

  • Thoracentesis

  • Mechanical ventilation

Types of spontaneous pneumothorax include:

  • Primary spontaneous pneumothorax → occurs without underlying lung disease.

  • Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax → occurs due to lung diseases (e.g., COPD, TB).

Other options:

  • Open pneumothorax → may occur spontaneously in some contexts but is more commonly traumatic.

  • Closed pneumothorax → can be spontaneous.

  • Tension pneumothorax → can develop as a complication of spontaneous pneumothorax.

Exam pearl:
Spontaneous pneumothorax = Primary + Secondary.
Iatrogenic and traumatic pneumothorax are non-spontaneous causes.

Medicine 03.question: ৪৮) MDR TB is resistant to......?
Medicine 03.exp:
MDR-TB (Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis) is defined as tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that is resistant to at least the two most important first-line anti-TB drugs:

  • Isoniazid (INH)

  • Rifampicin

Resistance to both INH and Rifampicin makes treatment more difficult and requires second-line anti-TB drugs.

Other options:

  • INH → MDR-TB includes resistance to INH, but not INH alone.

  • Rifampicin → MDR-TB includes resistance to Rifampicin, but not Rifampicin alone.

  • None of them → Incorrect.

Exam pearl:
MDR-TB = Resistance to INH + Rifampicin (HR resistance).
RR-TB = Rifampicin-resistant TB (with or without INH resistance).

Medicine 03.question: ৪৯) Which is the commonest organism of CAP?
Medicine 03.exp:
The commonest causative organism of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is the most frequent bacterial cause of CAP in both outpatient and inpatient settings.

Other options:

  • S. aureus → Can cause pneumonia, especially after influenza infection or in hospitalized patients, but it is not the commonest CAP organism.

  • N. meningitidis → Rare cause of pneumonia.

  • E. coli → More commonly associated with hospital-acquired pneumonia, aspiration, or pneumonia in debilitated patients.

Exam pearl:
Commonest organism of CAP → Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Commonest atypical pneumonia organism → Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

Medicine 03.question: ৫০) Antibiotic coverage in lung abscess should be given...?
Medicine 03.exp:
Lung abscess requires a prolonged course of antibiotics, usually 4–6 weeks, because the infection involves a localized collection of pus within lung tissue and requires time for clinical and radiological resolution.

Treatment typically includes:

  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobic organisms (e.g., clindamycin or beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations).

  • Duration is continued until there is significant clinical improvement and radiological resolution.

Other options:

  • 2–3 weeks → Usually too short for lung abscess.

  • 3–4 weeks → May be insufficient in most cases.

  • 6 months → Duration used for diseases like tuberculosis, not lung abscess.

Exam pearl:
Lung abscess antibiotic duration → 4–6 weeks (long-term therapy).
